extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and writers interested in literature, manners, and education (Spectator readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and aesthetic criteria for evaluating epic poetry and related moral/social commentary (character, fable, diction, and suitability of incidents), together with practical standards on education, sincerity, and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: contrasting virtues (courage vs piety)
rubrics_metrics.description: He compares Turnus and Æneas: 'He makes Courage the chief and greatest Ornament of Turnus; but in Æneas there are many others which out-shine it, amongst the rest that of Piety.' Turnus's ostentation and haughty language contrast with Æneas's reserved, defensive courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate heroic characters by the balance of virtues they display (e.g., ostentation vs composed duty). Consider how language, behaviour, and success/conduct together establish a hero's moral weight: 'If Equipage and Address make Turnus appear more couragious than Æneas, Conduct and Success prove Æneas more valiant than Turnus.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tradition/history to justify extraordinary incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgil takes matters of fact from Roman tradition and 'circumstanced them after his own manner' so that even seemingly ludicrous particulars (e.g., the Harpy prophecy that 'they should be reduced by Hunger to eat their very Tables') are retained because they were part of the transmitted history of Æneas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an epic includes incredible or violent machines/metamorphoses, check whether the poet preserves or adapts traditional/historical particulars — this can legitimate the extraordinary and make it 'appear the more natural, agreeable, or surprizing.' Examples: the Harpy prophecy and the fleet changing into water-nymphs (also found in Ovid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification of ludicrous particulars by appropriate narrator/agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgil makes the ludicrous line acceptable by placing it in the mouth of a young Ascanius (a boy): 'Such an observation, which is beautiful in the Mouth of a Boy, would have been ridiculous from any other of the Company.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether odd or comic details are qualified by the speaker or situation (age, authority, reliability) so they read as natural rather than absurd. Properly attributed utterances can transform a ridiculous report into a fitting characterizing detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition and contrivance of the fable (plot construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Disposition and Contrivance of the Fable' is called 'the principal Beauty' of Milton's ninth Book, which has more story and is fuller of incidents than other books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge an epic on the art of its plot arrangement: how incidents are sequenced, how much story is embedded, and whether the structure supports sustained interest. A skillful contrivance makes many incidents cohere into a principal beauty of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of authorial voice; filling the work with manners and characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton 'speaks as little as possible in his own Person, and, after the Example of Homer, fills every Part of his Work with Manners and Characters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer poems that show rather than tell: limit intrusive authorial commentary and instead let characters' actions, dialogues, and manners carry the poem's meaning and moral weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of imagery and description to the subject (tone and register)
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's 'Description of the Morning' is 'wonderfully suitable to a Divine Poem, and peculiar to that first Season of Nature' — e.g., earth breathing 'Morning Incense' and the pair joining 'vocal Worship to the Choir of Creatures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether images and descriptive language fit the poem's subject-matter and tone (the divine, the heroic, the pastoral). Appropriate, elevated imagery strengthens the poem's dignity; mismatched images weaken it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral delicacy and reasoned discourse in character dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam and Eve's dispute 'proceeds from a Difference of Judgment, not of Passion, and is managed with Reason, not with Heat: It is such a Dispute as we may suppose might have happened in Paradise, had Man continued Happy and Innocent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dialogues for plausibility and moral subtlety: conflicts should arise from believable differences of judgment, handled with reasoned argument rather than unmotivated passion, especially in elevated or sacred contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of similitudes (analogies) that are close and natural
rubrics_metrics.description: A noted similitude: the serpent 'rolling forward in all his Pride' leading Eve to destruction is praised as 'not only very beautiful, but the closest of any in the whole Poem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward analogies and similes that are vividly worked out and closely apt to the scene; such close comparisons increase naturalness and poetic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological realism in representing pleasure, guilt, and remorse
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's depiction of 'that secret Intoxication of Pleasure... and all those transient flushings of Guilt and Joy' and the subsequent 'flagging of Spirits, damps of Sorrow, and mutual Accusations' is praised as 'conceiv'd with a wonderful Imagination, and described in very natural Sentiments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how convincingly a poem renders inner states and moral consequences; subtle, natural portrayals of changing feeling increase the work's emotional truth and moral impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallels with classical authors as a defense against criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing Milton's passages in the same light as similar passages in Homer both sets off Milton's greatness and 'may be also guarded against the Cavils of the Tasteless or Ignorant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical parallels to contextualize innovations or seeming faults: similarity to respected models can justify bold devices and deflect superficial objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and truth over dissimulation in conduct and conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that 'Truth and Reality have all the Advantages of Appearance... Sincerity is true Wisdom' and that integrity is 'the shortest and nearest way to our End' — deceit requires continual props and is ultimately disadvantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a moral/social criterion: value sincerity because it is more secure, less troublesome, creates trust, and yields longer-lasting advantages than artifice; dissimulation is an eventual liability and makes one 'ridiculous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical education: teach small, useful accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: For most boys, 'many more Estates have been acquir'd by little Accomplishments than by extraordinary ones' — recommend practical geometry, writing English letters, accounts, shorthand, and punctual correspondence between pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor curricula that prioritize practical skills likely to be repeatedly useful in life and business (letter-writing, surveying, accounts) rather than pushing every pupil toward high literary genius; examples include cutting a dial, surveying an estate, or maintaining a letter correspondence to practice composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor education to natural talents; avoid forcing genius-mode on all
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'absurd to give a Lad the Education of one, whom Nature has not favour'd with any particular Marks of Distinction' — many boys should be taught practical arts rather than works of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess educational plans for fit with the pupil's capacities: prioritize useful, attainable accomplishments for the majority rather than a one-size-fits-all elite curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty as a social virtue linked to courage and magnanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Xenophon's account of Spartans: 'There was so much Modesty in their Looks... This Virtue, which is always join'd to Magnanimity, had such an influence upon their Courage...' The Spectator laments modern affectation of smartness and blustering airs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value modesty in demeanour as evidence of true courage and magnanimity; treat ostentatious displays of bravery or smartness as signs of affectation and social vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious piety (the Devotée) that disparages religion
rubrics_metrics.description: A Devotée 'disparages Religion by their indiscreet and unseasonable introduction of the Mention of Virtue on all Occasion[s]' — ostentatious behaviour (praying publicly to be observed, moral tracts displayed) makes virtue 'ridiculous' and deters others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral representation or social conduct, beware of characters or behaviors that turn virtue into theatrical display; such ostentation damages the credibility of genuine piety and can make religion 'not only unamiable, but also ridiculous.'
